prompt: Is there a way to measure our share of voice in AI chatbot answers?

brand.name: Cheap Seats
brand.about: Cheap Seats is an open-source, self-hosted tool that asks AI assistants a brand's buyer questions, grades whether they recommend the brand, and builds a ranked list of fixes.

answer:
Yes. A category of tools now does this, often sold as "AI visibility" or "GEO/AEO" tracking. They all use the same basic method, and you can also run it yourself on a spreadsheet.

## How it works
1. **Build a prompt set.** Write 50–200 questions your buyers actually ask, such as "best [category] for [use case]", "[you] vs [competitor]" and "how do I solve [problem]". Group them by funnel stage and persona.
2. **Run them across engines.** Cover ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, Google AI Overviews/AI Mode, Claude and Copilot. Showing up in one doesn't mean you show up in the others.
3. **Run each prompt several times, in fresh sessions.** The same prompt gives different answers from run to run, so a single result tells you very little.
4. **Score the answers:**
   - **Mention rate:** the % of answers that name you.
   - **Share of voice:** your mentions ÷ all brand mentions in your competitive set.
   - **Citation share:** how often your URLs are cited as sources.
   - **Position and sentiment:** whether you're listed first or fifth, and whether you're recommended or given caveats.
5. **Track the trend every week or month.** The direction over time tells you more than any one number.

## Tools worth shortlisting
I took these prices from recent comparison sites, and they don't all agree, so check them on each vendor's page.
- **Semrush AI Visibility Toolkit:** about $99/mo per domain, and you don't need a base Semrush plan. It's the easiest start if your team already uses Semrush. The entry tier has the lowest prompt limits.
- **Ahrefs Brand Radar:** from $199/mo for one platform, or about $699/mo for all platforms, plus the Ahrefs base plan. It draws on a large pre-built prompt index, so it's good for benchmarking against competitors without writing all your own prompts.
- **Peec AI:** roughly $80–100/mo to start, with higher tiers around $200–420. It's built for this job, priced for mid-market budgets, and does competitor share-of-voice dashboards well.
- **Profound:** the enterprise option. Plans reportedly start around $99–499/mo, but the cheapest covers ChatGPT only, multi-engine starts at about $399, and enterprise contracts are often $30K–100K+ a year. Choose it if you need depth, a lot of prompts, and executive reporting.
- Others to look at: Otterly, Superlines, AIclicks.

## Practical advice
- **Pilot first.** Run 30–50 prompts by hand, or with a cheap tool, for a month before you sign an annual contract.
- **Your prompt set is the measurement.** Write it to match real buyer questions, using sales calls and search data, and keep it fixed so the numbers can be compared over time.
- **Watch citation sources.** Knowing which third-party pages the chatbots cite (review sites, Reddit, listicles) is usually more useful than the share-of-voice number, because those are pages you can work to get onto.
- **Be skeptical of vendor claims.** Most of the published "guides" come from vendors, and Google rankings reportedly have little correlation with being cited in ChatGPT.

prompt: Is there a way to measure our share of voice in AI chatbot answers?

brand.name: Cheap Seats
brand.about: Cheap Seats is an open-source, self-hosted tool that asks AI assistants a brand's buyer questions, grades whether they recommend the brand, and builds a ranked list of fixes.

answer:
Yes. "AI share of voice" (also called AI visibility or GEO/AEO tracking) is now a standard metric with its own set of tools. The basic method is simple, and you can do it yourself or pay a tool to do it.

## How it works

1. **Build a prompt set.** Write 50–200 questions a buyer would really ask, such as "best [category] tools for [use case]," "[you] vs [competitor]," and "how do I solve [problem]." Mix unbranded category prompts with comparison prompts. The unbranded ones matter most.
2. **Run them on a schedule** across ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, Google AI Overviews/AI Mode, and Claude/Copilot if they matter to your audience.
3. **Score each answer.** Note whether you were mentioned, where you appeared in the list, whether your site was cited as a source, whether the tone was positive or negative, and which competitors showed up.
4. **Calculate share of voice:** your brand mentions ÷ all brand mentions in the category × 100. Track it over time against named competitors.

**Why to track each engine separately:** the engines disagree with each other a lot. One 2026 study found ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity and AI Overviews cited the same domains for only 3.8% of prompts, and named the same brands only about a third of the time. A blended number hides this, so report per engine.

## Tools

| Tool | Best for | Approx. price* |
|---|---|---|
| **Semrush AI Visibility Toolkit** | Teams already on Semrush. It's the cheapest way to start and sits next to your SEO data | ~$99/mo per domain |
| **Ahrefs Brand Radar** | Ahrefs users. It has a large pre-built prompt index, so you see share of voice without writing prompts first | Basic access on paid plans; full AI indexes cost a few hundred $/mo |
| **Peec AI** | Mid-market teams that want a dedicated tool with clean competitor share-of-voice dashboards and unlimited seats | ~€89–199/mo |
| **Profound** | Enterprise. It covers many engines with deeper citation and sentiment analysis | Entry tiers are cheap but limited to fewer models; higher tiers go through sales |
| **Otterly.AI, AthenaHQ, Scrunch** | Alternatives worth trialing | Varies |

*Published prices disagree a lot between review sites, especially for Profound and Ahrefs, so check the vendor pages before you budget.

## What I'd recommend

- **Start with what you already pay for.** If you have Semrush or Ahrefs, turn on their AI module and get a baseline this week.
- **If share of voice will be a KPI you report to leadership,** trial Peec AI and Profound side by side for 2–4 weeks using the same prompt set, then choose based on engine coverage and how well each one handles your competitor list.
- **Do a free version first if you want proof of value.** Run 30 prompts by hand each month across 3 engines and record the results in a spreadsheet. It's tedious, but it shows whether the metric is useful to you before you buy anything.

## Caveats to tell stakeholders about

- **Answers vary from run to run and are personalized.** Look at trends across many prompts and repeat runs, and don't react to a single answer.
- **Most tools query the engines' APIs or simulated sessions, not real user sessions.** The numbers show your relative position, not actual impressions.
- **Mentions without sentiment can mislead.** Track whether you're *recommended*, not just whether you're named.
- **Most "best tool" lists come from vendor blogs.** Treat their rankings and statistics as rough guides.

prompt: Do ChatGPT and Claude say different things about a product with web search on versus from training data alone, and how do I measure both?

brand.name: Cheap Seats
brand.about: Cheap Seats is an open-source, self-hosted tool that asks AI assistants a brand's buyer questions, grades whether they recommend the brand, and builds a ranked list of fixes.

answer:
Yes. **ChatGPT and Claude can describe a product differently with web search enabled versus using training data alone.** They can also differ from each other, and between repeated runs.

With search, answers can reflect newer pricing, features, reviews, competitors, and positioning. Without search, answers rely on what the model learned during training and any context you provide, which may be incomplete or outdated. Search can improve freshness, but it can also introduce misleading sources or overemphasize whichever pages it retrieves.

For a marketing lead, measure this as a four-condition comparison:

| Condition | What it measures |
|---|---|
| ChatGPT, search disabled | Product perception without retrieval |
| ChatGPT, search enabled | Product perception with access to current sources |
| Claude, search disabled | Product perception without retrieval |
| Claude, search enabled | Product perception with access to current sources |

**Search enabled doesn’t always mean search was used.** Record whether the assistant actually searched. If you explicitly require search, label that test “search required” and keep it separate from normal user behavior.

A practical testing process:

1. **Build 20–30 realistic prompts.** Include category discovery (“What tools help with X?”), recommendations, comparisons, pricing, capabilities, and objections. Include prompts that never mention your brand so you can measure discovery.
2. **Run each prompt in all four conditions, three to five times.** Use fresh conversations, consistent settings, and no personalization or prior brand context where possible. Record the date and model identifier.
3. **Save the complete answers.** For search runs, also save citations and any visible search activity. For a true no-search baseline, disable the tool; asking “don’t search” is a weaker control.
4. **Score against a dated product fact sheet.** Apply the same rubric to every answer.

Track these metrics:

| Metric | Practical measure |
|---|---|
| Brand visibility | Percentage of unbranded prompts mentioning your product |
| Recommendation rate | Percentage recommending your product |
| Positioning | Category, audience, use cases, and differentiators attributed to it |
| Accuracy | Correct, incorrect, outdated, or unverifiable product claims |
| Competitive framing | Competitors mentioned and reasons given for preferring them |
| Source coverage | Sources cited, including your own site and third parties |
| Consistency | How often findings recur across repeated runs |

Calculate the **search effect separately for each assistant**: search-on result minus search-off result. For example, if recommendation rate rises from 20% to 35%, report a **15-percentage-point increase**. Keep example answers alongside the numbers so you can explain what changed.

For tools, start with **Google Sheets or Excel**: both make a small pilot easy to audit. For repeatable testing at scale, use the **OpenAI API and Anthropic API**, with retrieval explicitly configured and logged. API results should be labeled separately from the consumer ChatGPT and Claude apps, whose surrounding instructions and search behavior may differ.

One limitation matters: **a no-search answer does not reveal exactly what training data contains**. You’re measuring observable behavior without retrieval—not proving that a particular page or fact was present in training.

prompt: Which questions should we track to measure AI visibility, and how many prompts do we need before the numbers mean anything?

brand.name: Cheap Seats
brand.about: Cheap Seats is an open-source, self-hosted tool that asks AI assistants a brand's buyer questions, grades whether they recommend the brand, and builds a ranked list of fixes.

answer:
**Start with 100–200 distinct buyer questions, tracked consistently across the AI platforms your customers use.** That’s a practical operating recommendation, not a statistical threshold. A smaller set can reveal gaps; a credible visibility percentage needs representative coverage and repeated observations.

**Which questions to track**

Build your list from sales calls, customer interviews, support tickets, site search, and search-query data. Use AI to expand that evidence, then review the suggestions.

| Question type | Example | What it measures |
|---|---|---|
| Problem discovery | “How can a small team reduce customer churn?” | Whether you enter the conversation early |
| Category recommendations | “Best customer-success software for a 20-person SaaS company?” | Whether you make the shortlist |
| Requirements and constraints | “Which tools integrate with Salesforce and cost under $500/month?” | Whether you appear for buyers you can serve |
| Comparisons and alternatives | “Alternatives to [competitor] for startups?” | Competitive consideration |
| Purchase objections | “What are the drawbacks of [brand]?” | Whether AI reinforces or resolves concerns |
| Brand accuracy | “Does [brand] support EU data residency?” | Whether your positioning and facts are correct |

Put roughly **70–80% of the panel into unbranded discovery and buying questions**, with the rest covering branded evaluation and accuracy. Treat that split as a starting point. Report the groups separately: asking about your brand practically guarantees a mention.

Cover your main buyer segments, use cases, and markets. Avoid filling the panel with slight rewrites of “best [category]”—that adds volume without much coverage.

**How many prompts make the numbers useful?**

Distinguish **unique questions** from **answer runs**. Running 100 questions three times on three platforms produces 900 answers, but still covers only 100 questions.

For perspective, these are approximate worst-case margins of error for a proportion under independent, representative sampling:

| Independent observations | Approximate 95% margin |
|---:|---:|
| 50 | ±14 percentage points |
| 100 | ±10 points |
| 200 | ±7 points |
| 400 | ±5 points |

These follow standard [sample-size calculations for proportions](https://itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/ppc/section3/ppc333.htm). **They are not automatic confidence intervals for an AI visibility dashboard:** handpicked prompts aren’t a random sample of all customer conversations, and repeated answers or related questions can be correlated. A 400-prompt panel can still be biased.

My practical setup would be:

- **Pilot:** 30–50 questions to find obvious omissions and inaccurate claims.
- **Working baseline:** 100–200 distinct questions, run on three separate days per reporting period to assess variability.
- **More precise reporting:** expand toward 400 questions when you need finer overall comparisons. Individual segment scores still need adequate coverage of their own.

Keep the panel, geography, language, and collection method fixed. Report platforms separately, document model changes, and establish several weeks of baseline before interpreting small movements.

**What to put on the dashboard**

Track unbranded **mention rate**, **recommendation rate**, **citation rate**, and **accuracy of important claims**, alongside the same measures for competitors. Define each denominator explicitly. Keep referral traffic and conversions alongside visibility so you can assess business impact.

For collection, **Ahrefs Brand Radar** is one option because its [custom prompt tracking](https://help.ahrefs.com/en/articles/13192745-how-to-set-up-custom-prompts-to-track-brand-visibility-in-ai-assistants) supports selected questions, platforms, locations, and scheduled refreshes. Its broader search-derived database can help discover gaps, but search demand is a proxy for AI conversation demand.

The defensible headline is: **“We appeared in 32% of answers across our tracked buyer-question panel.”** Calling that “32% of all AI searches” would overstate what you measured.

prompt: How can I see which web pages AI assistants rely on when they answer questions in my category?

brand.name: Cheap Seats
brand.about: Cheap Seats is an open-source, self-hosted tool that asks AI assistants a brand's buyer questions, grades whether they recommend the brand, and builds a ranked list of fixes.

answer:
You can see this in three ways: test the assistants yourself, pay for a monitoring tool, or check your own logs. Most teams start with the first and move to the second once they know which prompts matter.

## 1. Manual spot-checks (free, start here)

Write 20–50 prompts your buyers actually ask, such as "best [category] tools for mid-market," "[competitor] alternatives," or "how do I solve [problem]." Run them in:

- **Perplexity**, which shows numbered citations on every answer. It's the easiest place to see sources.
- **ChatGPT with search**. Click "Sources" to see the citation panel.
- **Google AI Overviews and AI Mode**. The cited links appear in the side panel.
- **Gemini, Claude (with web search), and Microsoft Copilot**, which all show linked sources.

Log the cited URLs in a spreadsheet. Within a day you'll see the patterns: which review sites (G2, Capterra), which Reddit threads, which listicles, which competitor pages, and whether your docs show up.

**Caveat:** answers vary by run, location, account history, and model version. Run each prompt several times and treat the results as directional.

## 2. AI visibility / "GEO" tracking tools (for ongoing monitoring)

These tools run your prompt set across assistants on a schedule and aggregate the cited domains and URLs:

- **Profound**: the most enterprise-grade option, with strong citation and source analysis across ChatGPT, Perplexity, AI Overviews, and others. A good fit if you have budget and need executive reporting.
- **Peec AI**: clean UI, good source and domain breakdowns, and reasonable pricing for mid-size teams.
- **Otterly.ai**: affordable and simple. A good first paid tool for tracking citations and brand mentions.
- **Scrunch AI** and **AthenaHQ**: these also track citations and add recommendations on what to fix.
- **Ahrefs Brand Radar** and **Semrush AI Toolkit / AI SEO**: worth checking first if you already pay for either suite, since the add-on may be enough.

What to look for: per-URL citation data (not just "you were mentioned"), competitor comparison, coverage of the engines your buyers use, and the ability to import your own prompts. This space changes fast, so confirm current engine coverage and pricing in a demo.

## 3. Your own data (shows when *your* pages are used)

- **Server or CDN logs.** Filter for AI user agents like `ChatGPT-User`, `OAI-SearchBot`, `PerplexityBot`, `Perplexity-User`, `Claude-User`, and `Google-Extended`. Live fetches by agents like ChatGPT-User usually mean a page was pulled to answer a question. Cloudflare's AI crawler analytics makes this easy if you're on Cloudflare.
- **GA4 referrals.** Look for traffic from `chatgpt.com`, `perplexity.ai`, `gemini.google.com`, `copilot.microsoft.com`, and `claude.ai`, and note which landing pages it reaches.

## Important limitation

All of these methods show **retrieval citations**, meaning the pages fetched live when answering. None can show what shaped the model's **training data**, which also influences answers. Being cited in search-backed answers is the part you can measure and influence.

## Suggested path

1. Spend a week on manual checks with about 30 prompts.
2. Identify the 10–20 domains cited most in your category.
3. Trial Peec AI or Otterly (or Profound if you're enterprise) to track that set monthly.
4. Put effort into the cited sources you can influence: review sites, comparison articles, Reddit and community threads, and your own docs and comparison pages.

prompt: How can I find out whether ChatGPT recommends my product when people ask about my category?

brand.name: Cheap Seats
brand.about: Cheap Seats is an open-source, self-hosted tool that asks AI assistants a brand's buyer questions, grades whether they recommend the brand, and builds a ranked list of fixes.

answer:
**Run a repeatable “buyer question” audit, then track it over time.** You can measure whether ChatGPT recommends your product for representative questions; that won’t tell you exactly what every customer sees.

1. **Build 20–30 questions your buyers actually ask.** Use sales calls, customer interviews, and search data. Include:
   - “What are the best [category] products for [audience]?”
   - “Which [category] works best for [use case] under [budget]?”
   - “What are alternatives to [competitor]?”

   Keep your own brand out of the discovery questions. Asking about your product by name tests awareness, not whether ChatGPT independently recommends it.

2. **Run each question in a fresh ChatGPT conversation.** Disable memory and custom instructions for a cleaner baseline. Record the date, model or mode, target country, and whether web search was used. Repeat each question several times across different days. Location and memory can affect ChatGPT’s search results, so keep conditions consistent. [OpenAI’s search documentation](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/9237897-searching-the-web-with-chatgpt)

3. **Score recommendations separately from mentions.** A spreadsheet is enough initially:

   | Measure | What to record |
   |---|---|
   | Recommendation rate | Percentage of tested answers that recommend your product |
   | Competitive presence | Which competitors appear alongside you or instead |
   | Message accuracy | Whether features, positioning, and pricing are correct |
   | Sources | Which pages ChatGPT cites when discussing your category |

   Save the full answers so you can inspect the context. Being mentioned as unsuitable shouldn’t count as a recommendation.

4. **Automate once you have a useful question set.**
   - **OtterlyAI** is worth testing for recurring prompt monitoring, brand mentions, and website citations. It also supports country-specific checks. [Monitoring details](https://help.otterly.ai/search-prompt-monitoring), [collection methodology](https://help.otterly.ai/how-otterlyai-collects-data)
   - **Profound** is worth evaluating if you need deeper analysis across topics and competitors, with captured responses, citations, and exportable data. [Answer Engine Insights](https://www.tryprofound.com/features/answer-engine-insights)

   Ask vendors whether they collect answers from ChatGPT’s website or an API, which modes they monitor, and whether you can inspect raw responses. Those choices affect how closely results reflect your buyers’ experience.

**Treat the dashboard as a sampled benchmark, not your actual market reach.** “Recommended in 35% of our tested answers” is defensible; “35% of ChatGPT users see us” is not. Pair the benchmark with ChatGPT referral traffic and a “How did you hear about us?” question to see whether visibility produces customers.

My recommendation: start with a two-week manual baseline, then trial a monitoring tool using the same questions. That gives you a concrete way to judge whether the tool earns its cost.

prompt: Which questions should we track to measure AI visibility, and how many prompts do we need before the numbers mean anything?

brand.name: Cheap Seats
brand.about: Cheap Seats is an open-source, self-hosted tool that asks AI assistants a brand's buyer questions, grades whether they recommend the brand, and builds a ranked list of fixes.

answer:
Track a mix of question types, weighted toward questions that don't name you. For the numbers to mean anything, plan on **roughly 150–300 prompts per segment you report on, each run 3–5 times per AI engine**. Below about 50 prompts, most week-to-week movement is noise.

## 1. Which questions to track

Build the prompt set from how buyers actually ask, not from your keyword list. Use roughly this mix:

| Bucket | Share | Examples | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Category / discovery** | ~35% | "Best [category] tools for [team size]", "What's the top [category] software for [industry]?" | Shows whether you're in the consideration set at all. This is your headline metric. |
| **Problem / job-to-be-done** | ~25% | "How do I reduce [pain]?", "How can a [persona] automate [task]?" | Earliest-funnel questions, where buyers don't yet know the category name. |
| **Comparison / alternatives** | ~20% | "[Competitor] alternatives", "[You] vs [Competitor]", "Is [Competitor] better than [You] for X?" | High purchase intent. Shows how you're positioned against rivals. |
| **Evaluation / purchase** | ~10% | "Does [You] integrate with Salesforce?", "[You] pricing", "Is [You] SOC 2 compliant?" | Tests accuracy. Wrong answers here cost deals. |
| **Branded / reputation** | ~10% | "What is [You]?", "Is [You] any good?", "[You] reviews" | Tests sentiment and how accurately you're described. Keep this share small, because it inflates visibility. |

Add **persona, industry, and use-case variants** to the core prompts ("…for healthcare," "…for a 10-person startup"). Assistants answer differently depending on these modifiers, and they're what make segment-level reporting possible.

**Where to source real prompts:**
- Sales call recordings from Gong or Chorus. Look at the questions prospects ask in discovery calls.
- Support tickets and onboarding questions.
- Google Search Console, especially long, question-style queries.
- Reddit, G2/Capterra reviews, and "People Also Ask" boxes.
- Win/loss notes, particularly the "who else did you look at" answers.

Freeze a core set so you can trend it over time. Refresh 10–20% per quarter in a separate bucket so the core numbers stay comparable.

## 2. What to measure for each prompt

- **Mention rate:** the percentage of responses that mention you. This is the primary KPI.
- **Share of voice:** your mentions divided by total mentions of you plus your tracked competitors.
- **Position:** first-mentioned or top-3 versus buried at the end of a list.
- **Citation rate:** how often your domain is linked as a source, and which third-party sites get cited instead. Those sites become your PR and content targets.
- **Accuracy and sentiment:** whether pricing, features, and positioning are described correctly.

## 3. How many prompts you need

AI answers are random, so mention rate behaves like a polling number with a margin of error:

| Responses in a segment | Margin of error (95%, at ~30% mention rate) |
|---|---|
| 50 | ±13 points |
| 100 | ±9 points |
| 300 | ±5 points |
| 1,000 | ±3 points |

**The catch:** re-running the same prompt doesn't count as fully independent data, because runs of one prompt are highly correlated. Your real sample size sits between the number of distinct prompts and the total number of runs, and usually closer to the number of prompts. So:

- **Prompts drive validity.** Extra runs mostly smooth out randomness within a single prompt.
- **Use 3–5 runs per prompt per engine.** Going beyond that adds little.
- **Size for every segment you report.** If you want "visibility in healthcare" on a slide, the healthcare segment needs its own ~100+ prompts.
- **Detecting change takes more data than measuring a level.** Reliably seeing a 5-point move between months takes several hundred prompts per segment. With a small set, report monthly or quarterly rolling averages rather than weekly swings.

**A practical starting setup:** 200–400 core prompts × 4 engines (ChatGPT, Google AI Overviews/AI Mode, Perplexity, plus Gemini or Claude) × 3 runs, measured weekly and reported monthly.

## 4. Tools

- **Profound:** enterprise-grade, with strong citation and source analysis and good coverage of the consumer interfaces. Best fit if you have budget and need executive reporting.
- **Peec AI:** mid-market and easy to set up. It's good for competitor share of voice and offers prompt suggestions.
- **Scrunch AI** and **AthenaHQ:** similar tier. Both pair monitoring with recommendations on what to fix.
- **Otterly.ai:** inexpensive. A good place to start if you want to validate the program before committing.
- **Semrush AI Toolkit** or **Ahrefs Brand Radar:** worth a look if you already pay for either. You get AI visibility alongside your SEO data, though the prompt control is less flexible.
- **Evertune:** built around large-sample statistical measurement. It's worth evaluating if statistical rigor is your main concern.
- **DIY via APIs:** the cheapest option for scale, but API responses often differ from the consumer apps people actually use, which add web search, personalization, and location. Use it as a supplement, not your only source.

Before buying, ask each vendor three things: how many runs they do per prompt, whether they query the consumer UI or the API, and whether they let you export raw responses. You want the raw responses so you can audit accuracy yourself.

**Bottom line:** most of your effort should go into building a realistic, mostly unbranded set of prompts sourced from real buyer language. Make it large enough per segment, at least 150, that a change in the numbers reflects something real rather than chance.

prompt: How can I find out whether ChatGPT recommends my product when people ask about my category?

answer:
You can test this, but you can’t see every recommendation ChatGPT makes to other users. The practical approach is to track a representative set of category questions over time.

1. **Build a list of 20–50 realistic buyer questions.** Include broad discovery (“What are the best tools for X?”), specific needs (“What works for a small team with Y constraint?”), comparisons, and alternatives to competitors. Use language from sales calls, customer interviews, and search queries.

2. **Run the questions in fresh ChatGPT conversations.** Avoid mentioning your brand in discovery questions—that would bias the test. Keep the model, search setting, and account conditions consistent, and record them. Repeat each question several times because answers vary. Test search-enabled answers separately if those matter to your buyers.

3. **Score the results in a spreadsheet.** Google Sheets or Excel works well for a first audit because you can review the actual answers alongside your metrics. Track:
   - Whether your product is mentioned.
   - Whether it is recommended, merely listed, or discouraged.
   - Which competitors appear.
   - Whether product descriptions are accurate.
   - Which sources are cited, when present.

4. **Repeat monthly using the same questions.** Report “our product was recommended in X% of these test responses,” rather than claiming that percentage represents all ChatGPT users. Look at results by buyer need; an overall average can hide where you win or disappear.

For larger monitoring programs, tools such as **Profound** or **Scrunch AI** are designed to track brand visibility in AI answers and can reduce manual collection. Before buying, ask how they collect ChatGPT results, which settings they cover, and whether you can inspect the underlying answers. **OpenAI’s API** can automate repeatable prompt testing, but its results shouldn’t be treated as identical to the consumer ChatGPT experience.

**Start with a manual baseline:** 25 questions, three fresh conversations per question, and a simple scorecard. That will show whether your main issue is missing mentions, inaccurate positioning, or competitors being preferred.

prompt: How often should we re-check whether AI assistants recommend us, and how do we track changes over time?

brand.name: Cheap Seats
brand.about: Cheap Seats is an open-source, self-hosted tool that asks AI assistants a brand's buyer questions, grades whether they recommend the brand, and builds a ranked list of fixes.

answer:
For most teams, run an automated check weekly, do a deeper manual review monthly, and do a full reset each quarter. Judge the results as trends over several runs and across many prompts. A single answer tells you very little, because the same prompt can produce different answers each time you ask it.

## How often to check

| Cadence | What to do | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Weekly (automated)** | Run a fixed set of 25–100 buyer-style prompts across ChatGPT, Gemini/AI Overviews, Perplexity, Claude and Copilot. Log whether you're mentioned, your position, which competitors appear and which sources are cited. | Often enough to catch real shifts without reacting to random variation. LLM Pulse uses weekly tracking as its default for this reason. ([LLM Pulse](https://llmpulse.ai/help-center/should-i-track-daily-weekly-or-monthly)) |
| **Monthly (manual)** | Read the actual answers for your top 10–15 prompts. Check whether the descriptions are accurate, what tone they take, and whether old pricing or features still show up. | Tools count mentions, but they don't reliably catch an answer that describes you wrongly. |
| **Quarterly** | Refresh the prompt set, add new competitors and markets, and check results against pipeline data such as AI referral traffic and "how did you hear about us" answers. | Buyer questions change, and AI results change a lot over a few months. One study reportedly found that about 70% of Google AI Overview results shifted over two to three months. That figure comes from a vendor blog, so treat it as directional. ([LLM Pulse](https://llmpulse.ai/help-center/should-i-track-daily-weekly-or-monthly)) |
| **Event-driven** | Run an extra check after a launch, rebrand, major PR moment, big model release or a competitor's move. | These are the times recommendations are most likely to move. |

Daily tracking is usually just noise. One cited study found ChatGPT gave different answers to the same questions about 10% of the time, even with randomness turned to its minimum. ([LLM Pulse](https://llmpulse.ai/help-center/should-i-track-daily-weekly-or-monthly))

## How to track changes over time

1. **Freeze a prompt set.** Split it into category prompts ("best X for Y"), comparison prompts ("you vs. competitor"), problem prompts, and prompts that name your brand. Only change it at the quarterly review, otherwise the trend lines stop being comparable.
2. **Run each prompt more than once per check** (3–5 times) and record the share of runs that mention you, not a yes/no.
3. **Track a few metrics:**
   - Mention rate (share of prompts or runs where you appear)
   - Average position when you're listed
   - Share of voice compared with your top 3–5 competitors
   - Citation sources: which of your pages, and which third-party sites like G2, Reddit or review sites, the AI is relying on
   - Accuracy and sentiment, scored by hand on the monthly review
4. **Keep notes alongside the data.** Log your content launches, PR and model updates so you can connect them to changes.
5. **Report 4-week rolling averages** to leadership instead of week-to-week numbers. All of this data is directional, because the AI companies don't publish query volumes and individual users' history changes what they see. ([Search Engine Land](https://searchengineland.com/llm-optimization-tracking-visibility-ai-discovery-463860), [Meltwater](https://meltwater.com/en/blog/how-to-track-llm-visibility))

## Tools

Pricing and engine coverage below come from comparison blogs and the sources disagree, so check vendor pages before buying.
- **Otterly.ai:** the cheapest way to start, reportedly about $29/month for 15 prompts. Good for a pilot.
- **Peec AI:** starts around $89–95/month. Strong for multi-market tracking (reportedly 115+ languages) and competitor share of voice.
- **Profound:** enterprise level, with the widest engine coverage and quote-based pricing. Worth it if this becomes a board-level metric.
- **Semrush AI Toolkit or Ahrefs Brand Radar:** convenient if you already pay for one of them.
- **HubSpot AI Search Grader:** free, good for a one-off baseline.

Several "best tools" listicles rank a tool called Mentionova first; those rankings look promotional, so I'd discount them. ([Rivo](https://www.rivo.io/blog/ai-visibility-tracking-tools), [Marketful](https://marketful.com/ai-visibility-tools), [TrustSignals](https://www.trustsignals.com/blog/the-top-12-tools-for-measuring-ai-visibility-and-brand-mentions-in-llms-2026), [MarketerHire](https://marketerhire.com/blog/top-tools-for-monitoring-brand-visibility-chatgpt))

**Practical start:** use the free HubSpot grader for a baseline this week. Then run Otterly or Peec for one quarter on about 30 prompts, checking weekly, with a 30-minute manual review each month. Decide on Profound only after you've seen whether the numbers move in ways you can act on.

prompt: What's the difference between being mentioned and being recommended in an AI answer, and how do I measure each?

brand.name: Cheap Seats
brand.about: Cheap Seats is an open-source, self-hosted tool that asks AI assistants a brand's buyer questions, grades whether they recommend the brand, and builds a ranked list of fixes.

answer:
**A mention means the AI includes your brand. A recommendation means it presents your brand as a suitable choice for the buyer’s needs.** Track them separately: visibility can rise without your brand becoming more likely to make the shortlist.

| | Mention | Recommendation |
|---|---|---|
| Example | “Acme sells project management software.” | “For a small agency that needs client approvals, Acme is a strong option.” |
| What it signals | Brand visibility | Buyer consideration and perceived fit |
| What doesn’t qualify | Appearing only on a linked source page | A neutral reference, criticism, or “Acme isn’t suitable for this need” |
| Core metric | **Mention rate:** answers naming your brand ÷ all sampled answers | **Recommendation rate:** buying-intent answers recommending your brand ÷ all sampled buying-intent answers |

A recommendation can be conditional—“choose Acme if you need X”—and still count. Record the condition; it tells product marketing which use cases the AI associates with your brand. Positive sentiment alone doesn’t establish a recommendation.

Also keep **citations** separate. Linking to your website means the AI used it as a source; it doesn’t necessarily mean it mentioned or endorsed your product. Current tracking tools distinguish mentions and citations, although their visibility and share-of-voice formulas differ. [Ahrefs metric definitions](https://help.ahrefs.com/en/articles/15501968-ai-visibility-metrics)

**Here’s how I’d measure it in practice:**

1. **Build a fixed set of buyer questions.** Start with 30–50 prompts covering discovery, use cases, comparisons, and purchase decisions. Use sales calls and customer research to choose them. Separate unbranded questions from prompts that explicitly name you—the latter can inflate visibility.
2. **Sample consistently.** Run the questions across the AI products your customers use, with consistent geography, language, and search settings. Repeat each prompt several times per reporting period. Save the full answers and dates.
3. **Label each answer.** Record brand mentioned, recommended, recommended first, reasons given, caveats, and citations. Count each brand once per answer. Review a sample manually if you automate classification.
4. **Report by buyer segment and use case.** An overall average can hide that you’re recommended for small businesses but excluded for enterprise buyers.

For example, across **100 buying-intent answers**, suppose your brand appears in 60 and is recommended in 25:

- **Mention rate:** 60%.
- **Recommendation rate:** 25%.
- **Recommendation among mentions:** 42%—25 of the 60 mentions involve an endorsement.

That third metric helps distinguish a visibility problem from a positioning problem. Track first-choice recommendations separately; being one of six suggested options is different from being the preferred choice.

For tools, **Ahrefs Brand Radar** is useful for discovering where your brand and competitors appear across a broad prompt database. **Profound Answer Engine Insights** supports ongoing prompt tracking with visibility, relative position, competitor share of voice, and citation data. For either, inspect the actual answers and apply your own recommendation rubric rather than treating a visibility score as endorsement. [Ahrefs overview](https://help.ahrefs.com/en/articles/11064852-what-is-brand-radar-and-how-to-use-it), [Profound prompt tracking](https://www.tryprofound.com/features/answer-engine-insights/prompt-tracking)

Treat these as **rates within your tracked sample**, not percentages of all customer AI conversations. Pair them with referral conversions and customer-reported discovery to assess business impact; neither mentions nor recommendations alone prove incremental revenue.

prompt: What's the best way to benchmark my brand's visibility in LLM answers against competitors?

brand.name: Cheap Seats
brand.about: Cheap Seats is an open-source, self-hosted tool that asks AI assistants a brand's buyer questions, grades whether they recommend the brand, and builds a ranked list of fixes.

answer:
The best approach is a **repeatable benchmark of real buyer questions**. Measure whether your brand appears, how it’s described, and which competitors get recommended across the AI tools your audience uses.

Start with a manageable baseline:

1. **Build 50–100 unbranded prompts from buyer needs.** Use sales calls, search queries, and customer interviews. Include category discovery (“best tools for…”), use cases, comparisons, and purchase criteria. Track branded questions separately—they inflate visibility.

2. **Test the same prompts across ChatGPT, Google Gemini, Perplexity, and Claude**, prioritizing platforms your customers use. Run each prompt in fresh conversations three times because answers vary. Keep language, geography, browsing settings, and model choice consistent.

3. **Score each response against a fixed competitor set.**

   | Metric | What it tells you |
   |---|---|
   | Mention rate | Percentage of answers that mention your brand |
   | Recommendation rate | Percentage that actively recommend your brand |
   | First recommendation rate | How often you’re the first brand recommended |
   | Competitive share of mentions | Your mentions divided by mentions of all tracked brands |
   | Accuracy and positioning | Whether your capabilities and differentiation are described correctly |
   | Citation sources | Which sites support the answer, where citations are available |

   Keep mentions and recommendations separate: an answer can mention you while recommending a competitor.

4. **Review results by buyer intent.** An overall score can hide strong category awareness but weak visibility for your most valuable use cases. Weight prompts by commercial importance, and retain an unweighted view for transparency.

5. **Repeat monthly using a fixed core prompt set.** Save full answers, citations, dates, and model details. Keep experimental prompts separate so changes in your test don’t masquerade as improvements.

For tools, I’d consider **Profound** for a dedicated AI visibility measurement program, **Scrunch AI** for visibility monitoring and investigating how AI systems understand your brand, or **Otterly.AI** for a smaller initial tracking pilot. Evaluate them using your own prompt set and confirm platform coverage, geography controls, repeat sampling, and raw-answer exports before committing. **Google Sheets** is sufficient for an initial manual baseline.

**My recommendation:** run a two-week pilot with 50 prompts, three priority platforms, and five competitors. Use the findings to identify specific gaps—missing recommendations, inaccurate positioning, or weak supporting sources—then measure whether addressing those gaps improves results.

Treat the benchmark as a consistent sample of visibility, not a measurement of every answer customers see. Pair it with referral traffic, conversions, and customer-reported discovery to judge business impact.

answer:
# Benchmarking Brand Visibility in LLM Answers

Treat this like brand tracking research, not SEO rank tracking. LLM answers are **probabilistic**, **personalized**, and **vary by model and surface**. You need a fixed prompt set, repeated sampling, and share-of-voice metrics over time.

## 1. Build the Prompt Set

This matters most. Aim for **50–200 prompts** that reflect real buyer questions, grouped by intent:

- **Category discovery:** "What are the best [category] tools for [use case]?"
- **Comparison:** "[You] vs [Competitor]", "Alternatives to [Competitor]"
- **Problem/solution:** "How do I solve [pain point]?" (no brand named)
- **Persona/segment:** "Best [category] for enterprise / startups / [industry]"
- **Branded:** "What is [You]? Is it good for X?" (checks accuracy and sentiment)

Pull prompts from sales call notes, G2 and Reddit questions, search query data, and your competitive battlecards. Unbranded prompts are where share of voice is actually won or lost.

## 2. Cover the Surfaces That Matter

At minimum, cover **ChatGPT, Google AI Overviews / AI Mode, Perplexity, Gemini, and Claude**. Add Copilot if you sell into Microsoft-heavy buyers.

Note that **API outputs differ from consumer app outputs**, which use web search, memory, and location. Prefer tools that capture the actual UI responses, or at least know which one you're measuring.

## 3. Sample Repeatedly

Run each prompt **multiple times (5–10+)** per model per cycle, weekly or biweekly. A single run is noise. Report rates, not anecdotes.

## 4. Track These Metrics

| Metric | What it tells you |
|---|---|
| **Mention rate** | % of answers that include your brand |
| **Share of voice** | Your mentions ÷ all tracked brand mentions |
| **Position/rank** | Listed first vs. fifth in a recommendation list |
| **Sentiment & framing** | "Best for enterprise" vs. "expensive, dated UI" |
| **Citation sources** | Which URLs the model cites (your site, G2, Reddit, competitor blogs) |
| **Accuracy** | Wrong pricing, features, or positioning |

**Citation sources are the most actionable metric.** They show which third-party pages you need to appear on or influence.

## 5. Tools

**Dedicated AI visibility platforms:**
- **Profound** is the enterprise leader. It has strong UI-level capture across engines, citation analysis, and an agent/crawler analytics view. It is pricey, but best if you need board-level reporting.
- **Peec AI** offers good value, a clean competitor share-of-voice dashboard, and multi-model coverage. It is popular with mid-market teams.
- **Scrunch AI** is strong on persona-based prompting and on spotting misinformation about your brand.
- **Otterly.AI** is affordable and simple. It is a good starting point for smaller teams.
- **AthenaHQ**, **Evertune** (statistically heavy, brand-marketer oriented), and **Goodie** are also worth a demo.

**Add-ons to SEO suites you may already own:**
- **Semrush AI Toolkit / AI SEO** and **Ahrefs Brand Radar** are convenient if your team already lives in these tools. Brand Radar has a large prompt dataset for discovering where competitors appear.
- **BrightEdge** and **Conductor** are options if you're already an enterprise SEO customer.

This market moves fast. Pricing and model coverage change quarterly, so verify current coverage in demos.

**DIY option:** If you have analyst support, script the prompts against the model APIs with web search enabled. Run N samples, use an LLM to extract brand mentions, rank, and sentiment, and dump the results into a spreadsheet or BI tool. It's cheap and fully transparent, but it misses consumer-app personalization and takes upkeep.

## 6. Make It Useful

- **Set a baseline**, then report **share of voice vs. top 3–5 competitors monthly**, segmented by intent and model.
- **Do gap analysis.** Find prompts where competitors appear and you don't, then check which sources the models cite for those answers.
- **Close the gaps** with comparison and alternatives pages, third-party reviews (G2, Capterra), Reddit and community presence, analyst and press coverage, and clear, structured product and pricing pages.
- **Tie it to outcomes.** Watch AI-referral traffic in GA4 (chatgpt.com, perplexity.ai, and similar) and add "How did you hear about us?" answers like "ChatGPT" to your attribution.

**Quick start:** Pick 75 prompts, run a 2-week trial of Peec AI or Profound alongside a manual spot-check, establish your baseline share of voice, and focus on the 10 highest-value prompts where you're absent.

prompt: How often should we re-check whether AI assistants recommend us, and how do we track changes over time?

brand.name: Cheap Seats
brand.about: Cheap Seats is an open-source, self-hosted tool that asks AI assistants a brand's buyer questions, grades whether they recommend the brand, and builds a ranked list of fixes.

answer:
**Check weekly at minimum; automate daily checks if AI recommendations matter to your pipeline. Review trends monthly.** That’s a practical starting cadence, rather than a universal benchmark.

| Frequency | What to do |
|---|---|
| Daily, automated | Track your highest-value buyer questions and flag sustained changes. |
| Weekly | Review recommendation rates, competitor movement, and a sample of actual answers. |
| Monthly | Report trends, investigate gains and losses, and choose content or positioning changes. |
| After major changes | Monitor daily following launches, pricing changes, major coverage, or assistant updates. Allow several weeks to assess the pattern. |

To make changes over time meaningful:

1. **Create a fixed benchmark of 30–50 prompts.** Use questions buyers actually ask: category recommendations, use cases, alternatives, and comparisons. Include unbranded questions such as “Which tools help a small team do X?” Branded questions alone won’t reveal whether assistants discover you.
2. **Keep testing conditions consistent.** Track each assistant separately, with the same prompt, language, location, and search settings. Use fresh conversations. Record the model/version when available and preserve the full answer and cited links.
3. **Measure recommendations separately from mentions.** Your primary metric should be **recommendation rate: the percentage of tracked answers that explicitly recommend you**. Also track competitor recommendation rates, prominence, cited sources, and inaccurate claims. A passing mention or citation doesn’t necessarily constitute an endorsement.
4. **Compare rolling periods.** Start with a two-to-four-week baseline, then compare rolling 28-day results with the previous period. Re-run apparent gains or losses before acting; individual answers can vary. Annotate launches, website edits, PR coverage, and tracking-method changes.
5. **Preserve your benchmark.** Add new prompts in a separate cohort so changing the question mix doesn’t create an artificial performance jump.

For tooling, shortlist:

- **Ahrefs Brand Radar** if you already use Ahrefs or want flexible scheduling. Its custom prompt tracking supports daily, weekly, or monthly checks across assistants and locations. [Ahrefs documentation](https://help.ahrefs.com/en/articles/13192745-how-to-set-up-custom-prompts-to-track-brand-visibility-in-ai-assistants)
- **Semrush AI Visibility Toolkit** if your team already reports through Semrush. It provides daily custom-prompt updates and integrates with its reporting tools. [Semrush documentation](https://www.semrush.com/kb/1496-getting-started-with-ai-visibility-toolkit)

Before buying, trial your own prompts and verify how the tool distinguishes a mention from a recommendation, and whether its collection method reflects the assistant experience your buyers use.

Your monthly dashboard can stay simple: **recommendation rate by assistant and use case, competitor comparison, change versus the previous 28 days, and three representative answers explaining the movement.** Treat those results as visibility within your tracked sample—not market-wide reach or proof of revenue impact.
